implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: one channel object that owns a FIFO buffer plus the delivery rule 'exactly one receiver takes each message'. Producers write to the channel, consumers take messages in a loop, and the channel (not the sender) decides which consumer gets a given message; attaching several consumers buys throughput, not copies. Bound the buffer so a slow consumer applies backpressure instead of growing memory, define the end-of-stream marker (close call or poison message), and state the delivery guarantee (at-most-once vs at-least-once) before writing consumers, because redelivery makes idempotency their job.
code_sketch:
channel = open_channel(name, capacity=100)      # provider: in-process queue or broker queue
producer.send(channel, message)                  # sender names the channel, not a receiver
loop:
    msg = channel.receive()                      # blocks/awaits; exactly one consumer gets it
    handle(msg); channel.ack(msg)                # ack AFTER handling (at-least-once)
# scaling: attach several consumers to the same channel (Competing Consumers)
pitfalls: Letting the sender choose or remember a consumer destroys the decoupling the pattern exists for.
Not defining the end-of-stream condition (close signal or poison message) leaves consumers blocked at shutdown.
Treating an at-least-once channel as exactly-once: redelivery after a crash re-executes non-idempotent handlers.

Wrong move: Put independent services in one Kafka consumer group -> partitions are load-balanced and each service sees only a subset -> instead assign each independent subscriber its own group ID (or use a separate queue or subscription).
